title: How Do Anteaters Eat 30,000 Ants a Day With No Teeth? 🐜
description:
How do anteaters eat without teeth? See how a giant anteater's two-foot sticky tongue, roof-of-the-mouth crush and muscular stomach handle up to 30,000 ants and termites a day.

Sources:
https://animals.sandiegozoo.org/animals/giant-anteater
https://seaworld.org/animals/facts/mammals/giant-anteater/
https://a-z-animals.com/articles/the-science-behind-how-anteaters-feed/

Animated in the Cut-Paper Diorama style.
pinned_comment: If you had to eat 30,000 of something with zero teeth, what would you pick?
script: Zero teeth, but it'll out-eat you, thirty thousand ants a day. Meet the giant anteater. First, big claws rip open the nest. Then out comes the tongue, two feet long, flicking up to a hundred and fifty times a minute. It's covered in tiny backward spines, and thick, sticky spit, so ants come along for the ride. With no teeth to chew them, it crushes them against the roof of its mouth, and a very muscular stomach pulverizes the rest. Scientists think swallowed grit helps too, a bit like a bird's gizzard. The clever part? It stays about a minute at each mound, then moves on, before the ants can fight back. So if you had to eat thirty thousand of something, with zero teeth, what would you pick?
key_facts: Giant anteaters have no teeth (San Diego Zoo, SeaWorld, LA Zoo)
Eat up to 30,000 ants and termites a day (San Diego Zoo, SeaWorld)
Tongue about 2 feet long, flicked up to 150 times a minute (San Diego Zoo, SeaWorld)
Tiny backward-pointing spines and sticky saliva (San Diego Zoo, SeaWorld)
Crushes insects against the roof of the mouth; very muscular stomach pulverizes the food (San Diego Zoo)
Swallowed grit may help grinding, stomach compared to a bird's gizzard (A-Z Animals, Encyclopedia.com)
Feeds at one mound for about a minute before moving on (San Diego Zoo)
